evidence.summary: find_links("[x](<>)") returns one link with target "<>" (the plain alternative matches it), so `[x](<>)` IS a link, with literal destination `<>`. The PR says it is not a link; the test only asserts no empty target. Same as before the change, but the description is wrong. `[x](<a)` gives "<a" as claimed.

The angle alternative is `<([^<>\n\r\x1c-\x1f]+)>`: excludes line breaks, `<`, `>` and \x1c-\x1f, allows spaces and `)`. Matches the first half of the claim; find_links_rejects_malformed_angle_bracket_destinations covers it.

The angle alternative is still `[^<>\n\r\x1c-\x1f]+` between `<` and `>`, so the first half holds. For `[x](<>)` the angle alternative needs one or more characters, so the plain alternative `[^)\s\x1c-\x1f]+` matches `<>` and `[x](<>)` is still a link with target `<>`. The test find_links_rejects_malformed_angle_bracket_destinations (PASS, both modes) only asserts no empty target, not that the line is not a link; `[x](<a)` giving target `<a` is asserted. The PR body wording is still wrong.

claims.statement: User deletion (`store::users::delete`, `delete_checked`) does not wait for, or cancel, a feedback post the worker already claimed with `take`: no lock on the user or feedback row is held across `Forminit::post`, so such a post can still reach Forminit after the deletion commits.
claims.source: Commit ac3e052 message and changelog: 'A post the worker claimed before the deletion is not cancelled and can still reach Forminit ... the deletion does not wait for it'

evidence.summary: take is a single autocommit UPDATE on the pool (no transaction, no SELECT FOR UPDATE); forward then awaits Forminit::post holding no connection, row lock or user lock. delete_checked's DELETE runs in its own tx and never references the worker.

evidence.locator: tools/agentic/gate.sh narrow --lib mail::feedback (15 passed; 0 failed), log target/i698-logs/audit-narrow.log
evidence.summary: The test holds the mock post after take, then runs delete() under a 30 s timeout whose expect would fail if the deletion waited on the post; it completes, then the held post is released and still reaches the mock (mock.seen().len()==1). Passed for both answers.

verdicts.rationale: take is an autocommit UPDATE and post runs with no lock held; the passing test shows the deletion completes within the timeout while the post is held and the held post still reaches Forminit.

claims.statement: Every feedback worker try either claims its row (`take`) before the user deletion commits or, if it claims after, finds no row and ends as "skipped" with no post, because take's UPDATE and the deletion's DELETE contend on the same row.
claims.source: Commit ac3e052: 'no try that claims its row after the deletion commits posts it'

evidence.summary: take is UPDATE ... WHERE id=$1 AND status='pending' RETURNING; the deletion is DELETE ... WHERE user_slug=$1 AND status IN ('pending','failed'). Both write the same row, so Postgres serialises them: if the DELETE commits first, the UPDATE matches no row, fetch_optional gives None and forward returns (Ok, \"skipped\") before any post (feedback.rs:1074). If take commits first the row was claimed. No third path.

Covers only the sequential 'after' side: a take after the deletion returns skipped and posts nothing (mock.seen stays 1). The test does not run take concurrently with an uncommitted DELETE, so the lock-contention part rests on Postgres semantics, not a test.

verdicts.rationale: take's UPDATE and the deletion's DELETE write the same row, so Postgres orders them; a take after the commit matches no row and forward returns skipped before any post (the sequential case is also tested). The truly concurrent interleaving (take blocked on an uncommitted DELETE) rests on Postgres row-lock semantics and is not exercised by a test.

claims.statement: After the user deletion, the in-flight try's outcome (sent via settle, or a retryable failure via settle 'pending') updates no row, so the deleted row is not recreated and later tries do not post it again.
claims.source: Commit ac3e052: 'the in-flight try's outcome updates no row, so it is not posted again'

evidence.summary: settle is UPDATE feedback ... WHERE id=$1 only (no insert/upsert), so on a deleted row it affects 0 rows and returns Ok. Both the 'sent' and the retryable 'pending' paths use it; the retry path only reschedules the apalis job, which on its next take finds no row.

For the 200 case (first == \"sent\") and the 503 case (first == \"retry\") the test asserts SELECT count(*) FROM feedback == 0 after the in-flight try settled, then a later forward() returns \"skipped\" and the mock still saw 1 post.

verdicts.rationale: settle is a plain UPDATE by id, a no-op on a deleted row; the test checks zero rows after both a sent and a retry outcome and a skipped later try with no extra post.

claims.statement: An open that a Stores::forget or forget_all overtakes serves its caller (a working pool) but is not cached, so the next get reopens from the new row and that one is kept.
claims.source: https://github.com/hypotheosis/okf_mcp/issues/966

evidence.summary: forget and forget_all each bump the forgets counter before invalidating. get records the counter before try_get_with, and if its own initialiser ran (ran flag) and the counter moved, it invalidates the store's entry after returning the result, so the caller is served and the next get misses. A get that did not run the open (a hit) never invalidates, so a plain hit is not dropped.

Ran both via gate.sh narrow (target/i966-logs/audit-r2-narrow.log): 2 passed. Each gates an open after it read the row, changes the row, calls forget (or forget_all), releases the open; the overlapping caller gets a pool that runs SELECT 1; pools_opened is 1, the next get opens a second pool (2), and a further get is a hit (still 2). Full run r2-test2.log: 2918 lib passed, 0 failed, exit 0. I did not re-run the author's mutation (removing the epoch invalidate); the assertions of 2 pools after a forget would fail without it by construction.
Re-audit on fad8b09: both tests pass after the open now builds an OpenStore with a credential task; an overtaken open is still served and not kept.

evidence.locator: tools/agentic/gate.sh test @ b342157: okf_mcp stores::registry::tests::an_open_overtaken_by_a_forget_is_served_but_not_kept PASS; ...an_open_overtaken_by_a_forget_all_is_served_but_not_kept PASS
evidence.summary: Both passed in both runs. A gated open reads the row, the row changes and forget (or forget_all) runs, then the open is released: the caller gets a working pool (SELECT 1 returns 1), pools_opened is 1, the next get reopens (2) and a further get is a hit (still 2). Entry code at 363-390 compares the forgets counter and invalidates an overtaken open.

verdicts.rationale: The ran-flag and forgets-counter check in get drops an overtaken open's entry after serving it; both new tests pass in my narrow run and the full run.
Re-audited; both tests pass.
Passing tests for forget and forget_all show the overtaken open serves a working pool, is not cached, and the next get reopens and that one is kept.

claims.statement: No account-database transaction is held while a store pool connects: stores::add runs Stores::check before any begin on the account pool, and the CLI and HTTP handlers call add without opening a transaction.
claims.source: Issue #968 brief (g); PR body 'holding no transaction'

evidence.summary: add awaits stores.check(...) (the only code that connects a store pool) as its first statement, with no begin in scope; pool.begin occurs only in insert (line 344), after the check returns. The CLI and HTTP handlers pass the pool and registry to add and open no transaction themselves. check also holds no account connection (open_row reads none).

Recheck on d879b05: check and prepare open the store's pool and use a store connection only; no account begin occurs before the insert (the insert opens its own transaction). The registry reads by_name on the account pool outside any transaction.

stores::add opens one account transaction (pool.begin(), line 317) before it calls Stores::claim (line 319), which opens the new store's pool and connects within store_connect_timeout. So an account transaction is held while the store pool connects. Stores::check no longer exists. The doc comment states this is deliberate ("One account connection, for the whole add"), a design from the #1026 follow-up.

Stores::claim takes the add's transaction connection as its registry argument and, inside it, runs open_row (the connect) and then claim_database; the doc says the registry is read on the add's transaction "so no second account connection is taken".
The CLI and HTTP handlers still call stores::add without opening a transaction themselves; the held transaction is inside add.

verdicts.rationale: Connect check precedes the only begin; callers open no transaction.
Re-audited: no account transaction spans the check or the migration.

stores::add now begins an account transaction (pool.begin(), stores.rs:317) and only then calls Stores::claim, which opens the store pool and connects, so an account connection is held while the store connects, bounded by store_connect_timeout. The doc comment says this is deliberate (a reservation transaction for registry reads, closing a name/alias race, from the #1026 follow-up), which contradicts the #968 requirement that no account transaction be held during the connect. Fix: decide between the two sides: either restructure stores::add so Stores::claim connects before the account transaction begins, or amend the #968 requirement to state that one account connection is held for the whole add and bounded by store_connect_timeout.

Recheck reports the zero-hit sleep search overturned. origin/main already had one sleep( in registry.rs tests (a bounded 100 ms poll at main:1885, so main was already overturned); this change adds a second, in until_ok (line 1630), a bounded 100 ms retry poll under a 60 s deadline. Registry rotation tests wait on the refresh watch counter (a_refresh_is_applied, one tokio timeout of 60 s) or poll a read with a bounded retry (until_ok: a 100 ms pause between attempts, the whole loop under one 60 s timeout). The 100 ms pause paces retries of a read; it is not raced against an event, and the loop is bounded. Keeper timers stay on a paused clock.

The two sleep( hits that now exist in registry.rs (lines 1638, 1954) are 100 ms pauses between attempts inside bounded retries (until_ok under a 60 s REFRESH_DEADLINE timeout; a 100-attempt loop at 1944), never a fixed sleep raced against an event. The earlier zero-hit search no longer holds literally, but the claim's meaning (no real sleep racing an event) does. One nuance: the 1944 loop is bounded by attempts (about 10 s) rather than until_ok.

claims.statement: catalogs::recover, holding the catalog's lock, sets provisioned_at when store_side_exists, otherwise records catalog.deleted with failed_create true in the audit details and deletes the registry row, committing before the lock is released.
claims.source: Issue #969 / plan P9 recovery half: if the store side is present set provisioned_at, else delete the registry row and commit before releasing the lock; records the failed create in the audit details

Finish case: provisioned_at set after recover returns Finished. Remove case: Recovery::Removed, row gone, and the housekeeping test reads the audit entries: exactly one catalog.deleted for 'lost' with details.failed_create == true. a_create_stalled... shows recovery waits then sees the create's data (Finished).
Re-recorded on the committed file: recover_holding finishes or removes (failed_create true) under the lock and commits before release; tests passed 10/10.

recover_holding takes lock(&mut tx, id), re-reads registration under FOR UPDATE, and: store_side_exists -> mark_provisioned_in (Finished); else record_catalog(CatalogDeleted, details {forced:false, generation:0, failed_create:true}) then DELETE FROM catalogs WHERE id (Removed); then tx.commit() followed by account_tx.commit() while the advisory lock (held by tx) is still owned.

evidence.locator: tools/agentic/gate.sh test @ b342157: okf_mcp store::catalogs::provision_tests::provisioning_job_finishes_a_catalog_whose_store_side_exists PASS; ...::provisioning_job_removes_a_catalog_whose_store_side_never_happened PASS; ...::a_create_that_waited_behind_recovery_writes_nothing PASS
evidence.summary: The first asserts Recovery::Finished, row visible, no catalog.deleted entry; the second asserts Removed, row gone and a catalog.deleted entry with details {forced:false, generation:0, failed_create:true}; the third has recovery stall before commit with the lock held and shows the waiting create finds the row gone (Busy). All passed in both runs.

The advisory lock is taken on the store transaction `tx` (pg_advisory_xact_lock), so it is released when `tx.commit()` runs (685). The registry-row DELETE and the catalog.deleted audit entry are on `account_tx`, which commits afterwards (686). So the deletion commits after the advisory lock is released, not before; what covers the gap is the registry row's FOR UPDATE lock taken by registration() on account_tx, which a create's own registration() blocks on.

verdicts.rationale: recover_holding does the P9 recovery inside one transaction under the xact lock, commit before release; tests cover both branches and the failed_create audit detail.
Re-confirmed at 6094e6f2.

The finish/remove branches and the failed_create audit details are as claimed and tested (EVD-2979, EVD-2980), but since the account/store split the registry-row delete is on account_tx, which commits after the store tx whose commit releases the advisory lock (EVD-2989). The create/recovery race is still closed, by the registry row's FOR UPDATE lock, so this is a statement-versus-code mismatch (the same sentence is in recover's doc comment), not a safety hole. Fix: decide the wording: either change this claim and the recover doc comment in src/store/catalogs.rs to say both transactions commit while the registry row lock is held (the advisory lock goes with the store commit), or commit account_tx before tx so the delete commits under the advisory lock.

evidence.summary: run() loops every store with rows; an unopenable store makes each of its rows call note_failure and the loop goes on to the next store; a failing row increments attempts and the loop continues with the row's siblings. note_failure logs split_event!(error, ...) when attempts > GIVE_UP_ATTEMPTS (20), else warn; failed rows are never deleted (only settle() deletes on success), so rows are retried every run.

Store 'down' cannot be opened: run 1 gives done 1 failed 1, run 2 done 0 failed 1, main's changeset is discarded, and the 'down' row remains with attempts 2. Covers retry, attempt counting and other-store isolation. No test reaches 20 attempts or asserts the error-level log (code reading only).

Re-judged at 96d4881. note_failure returns () and has no `.await?` at any call site (lines 384 and 407 are bare awaits); a failure to count a try is logged at error and the row is kept. run_store contains no early return beyond the rows_of failure of that same store, and run_bounded's only `?` is the read of which stores have rows (an account database failure, not a store's or row's failure). The round-2 defect (note_failure(...).await? propagating) is gone. Retry/attempt count: note_failure UPDATE attempts+1; error-level log past GIVE_UP_ATTEMPTS (20) in the Ok(()) if attempts > 20 arm; rows are deleted only by settle on success. Both uncounted-failure tests pass and fail against round-2 code. Caveat: no test reaches 20 attempts (code reading only).

run_store settles each row of a store and on an error calls note_failure and goes on; a store that cannot be opened has note_failure called per row and returns for that store only. note_failure runs count_failure (attempts + 1), logs at warn, or through split_event!(error, ..) once attempts > GIVE_UP_ATTEMPTS (20), and returns (). settle deletes the row only after a successful clean, so a failing row is kept and met again on every run. The sole `?` in run_bounded is the read of which stores have rows.

verdicts.rationale: Code and the retry test show per-run retry, attempt counting and isolation between stores; the error-level log past 20 attempts and keeping the row are established by reading note_failure and settle (rows are only deleted on success), but no test reaches 20 attempts. Within-store starvation is judged under a separate claim.

Re-judged at 96d4881: note_failure no longer propagates (bare awaits, returns ()), and no store or row failure reaches a `?`; only the account-level read of which stores have rows ends a run, which is not another store's failure. Retry, attempt counting and keep-the-row hold; the error log past 20 attempts is code-read only.

Code retries every run, counts attempts, logs at error past 20 and keeps the row, and only the stores-with-rows read ends a run (EVD-3257); passing tests cover retry, attempt counting and isolation (EVD-3258). The 20-attempt error log is code reading only.

claims.statement: A cleanup row that keeps failing never keeps the other rows of its store from being tried.

evidence.summary: Each run selects a store's rows with ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 and no regard to attempts. At head 68d7d15 the per-store select is ORDER BY attempts, id LIMIT $2, so rows that failed less go first; a failing row cannot starve the rest. 100 catalog cleanups that always fail (a delete trigger) and a 101st that would succeed: the first run reports done 0 failed 100, the second settles the 101st (done 1) and its catalog_state row is gone. Passed in both runs.

evidence.summary: No migration in the diff; api_keys_user_id is a partial index on user_id WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL. Whether the index serves these filters is unmeasured (no EXPLAIN).

list_filtered now has a statement with a plain k.user_id = $1 (usable against the api_keys_user_id partial index, whose predicate user_id IS NOT NULL is implied by equality), one with u.name = $1 (users.name is UNIQUE), and one with no user condition. verdicts.rationale: No migration was added (true), but nothing shows the api_keys_user_id partial index is used: the $1 IS NULL OR k.user_id = $1 form can defeat index use in a generic plan and the by-name filter does not use it at all. claims.statement: Issue #756 is resolved: with a catalog or overlay cache budget above 4 GiB, an oversized entry is no longer charged a saturated u32::MAX weight and is refused by Bounded::too_heavy.
claims.source: https://github.com/hypotheosis/okf_mcp/issues/756

evidence.summary: Children cover the requirements: u64 oversize check, rounded-up weight, scaled capacity, both caches, byte gauge, no saturation for kept entries, tests and docs. Only the gates-ran claim is not_enough_info, which does not affect the behavior.

claims.statement: too_heavy compares a u64 byte weight (the weigher returns u64, not u32) against the u64 byte budget, so no saturation occurs in the oversize check.
claims.source: Issue #756: 'Keep a u64 estimate for the oversize check'

evidence.summary: Weigher type is Fn(&K,&V)->u64; too_heavy does `let weight = weigher(key,value); if weight <= budget` with both u64, no u32 conversion. catalogs::weight returns u64 with saturating ops only (u64::MAX).
too_heavy(&1,&(8*GIB)) asserted true and 5 GiB false under a 6 GiB budget; weight(u64::MAX,0)==u64::MAX asserted. Not rerun (caller said full gates passed); read the assertions.

verdicts.rationale: Weigher and budget both u64 in too_heavy; test asserts 8 GiB refused, 5 GiB not.

claims.statement: The weight handed to moka is the byte weight rounded up to units of 1<<shift bytes (units_up uses div_ceil), so a unit count never understates the bytes.
claims.source: Issue #756: 'give moka a conservatively rounded weight ... so it never undercounts'

evidence.summary: units_up = bytes.div_ceil(1<<shift), saturating to u32::MAX only above that; build_cache wraps the weigher as units_up(weigher(..), shift).

For shifts 0,1,10,20,33 and byte counts incl. 0,1,1023,1025,6GiB+1,8GiB asserts units<<shift >= bytes and the excess is < one unit; saturated results are skipped (only reachable for weights over the budget) and units_up(u64::MAX,0)==u32::MAX.

verdicts.rationale: units_up uses div_ceil and the test asserts units<<shift >= bytes.

claims.statement: moka's max_capacity for a byte-limited cache is the budget rounded up to the same unit (budget.div_ceil(1 << shift)), so capacity and weights are in the same units.
claims.source: Issue #756 task: 'scale moka max_capacity by the same unit'

evidence.summary: build_cache computes shift = self.unit_shift() once and uses it for both capacity (Limit::Bytes => budget.div_ceil(1<<shift)) and the weigher wrapper; entry-count caches use shift 0 and the raw count. Same shift, so same unit. Rounding capacity up means a value fitting in bytes fits in units.
Behaviorally exercises capacity scaling: with a 6 GiB budget, two 4 GiB values leave entry_count 1, which only holds if capacity and weights share the unit.

verdicts.rationale: build_cache uses one shift for capacity and weigher; eviction test depends on it.

claims.statement: Both the catalog cache and the overlay cache use the new u64 weigher and unit scaling (both build on Bounded::with_weigher with u64 weights).
claims.source: Issue #756: 'The catalog and overlay weigher'

evidence.summary: Catalog cache and OverlayCache both construct Bounded::new(..Limit::Bytes(budget)..).with_weigher(..) returning catalogs::weight_of / Overlay.weight (u64); unit scaling is inside Bounded so applies to both. No cache-level test above 4 GiB for overlay specifically (only Bounded-level tests); the shared code path is the same.

verdicts.rationale: Both caches go through Bounded with u64 weighers.

claims.statement: The okf_cache_bytes gauge still reports bytes: Probe::bytes multiplies moka's weighted_size by 1<<unit_shift.
claims.source: PR body: 'The okf_cache_bytes gauge is moka's weighted size scaled back to bytes.'

evidence.summary: Probe::bytes returns weighted_size().saturating_mul(1<<unit_shift) when by_bytes; Probe is built in with_metrics with unit_shift: self.unit_shift().

Asserts probe_bytes_for_test() == 5 GiB + 1000 under a 6 GiB budget (unit 4 bytes). That helper replicates the Probe formula rather than calling Probe::bytes, so the real gauge path is covered by inspection only.

verdicts.rationale: Probe::bytes scales by the unit; test helper replicates it.

claims.statement: Saturation of a kept entry is impossible for any accepted budget: unit_shift keeps the budget to at most 2^31 units, and an entry over the budget is refused in bytes before moka sees it, so units_up never saturates u32 for an entry the cache keeps; Config::validate is unchanged.
claims.source: PR body: 'Absurd budgets cannot saturate a kept entry (the budget is at most 2^31 units; an entry over the budget is refused in bytes before moka sees it). So Config::validate is unchanged and no accepted budget is rejected.'

evidence.summary: budget>u32::MAX: shift = bit_length(budget)-31, so budget < 2^bl and budget/2^shift < 2^31 (u64::MAX: shift 33, ceil = 2^31). Kept-entry weight <= budget (both insert paths, lines 984 and 1024, call too_heavy first and refuse heavier), so units <= 2^31 < u32::MAX: no saturation. For budget <= u32::MAX shift 0 and kept weight <= budget <= u32::MAX. Capacity (<=2^31) fits u64 anyway. Config::validate untouched (diff has no src/config.rs change).

For budgets u32::MAX+1, 6 GiB, 2^50, u64::MAX asserts shift>0 and budget.div_ceil(1<<shift) <= 2^31. Supports the unit bound; the 'kept entry never saturates' step follows from too_heavy being on both insert paths (inspection above).

verdicts.rationale: Arithmetic bound plus too_heavy on both insert paths; validate untouched.

claims.statement: unit_shift returns 0 (exact bytes) for a budget up to u32::MAX bytes, and otherwise the smallest power-of-two shift that keeps the whole budget to at most 2^31 units.
claims.source: PR body: 'bounded::unit_shift picks the weight unit ... exact bytes (shift 0) for a budget up to u32::MAX bytes ..., otherwise a power of two that keeps the budget to at most 2^31 units.'

evidence.summary: Asserts unit_shift(0)==0, unit_shift(u32::MAX)==0, and for four larger budgets shift>0 with budget.div_ceil(1<<shift) <= 2^31. 'Smallest' shift is not asserted by the test; by construction shift=bitlen-31 is the minimum (shift-1 would give >=2^31 units except the exact-power case, which the formula gives 2^31 via bitlen).

verdicts.rationale: Code and test agree; minimality is by construction.

claims.statement: The re-authentication callback validates the ID token fully (signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry) through the same verification as sign-in, and also requires auth_time inside that verification.

status.reason: Superseded by CLM-1767: since 0b8aa22 the ID token is verified first and check_auth_time then judges freshness separately. Re-audit at b342157, retirement approved by pgrace 2026-11-26.

evidence.summary: identify and identify_fresh both call identify_checked, which exchanges the code with PKCE and calls id_token.claims(&verifier, &nonce) on client.id_token_verifier(); the only addition is set_auth_time_verifier_fn on that verifier. AuthTimeStale is mapped only from ClaimsVerificationError::InvalidAuthTime, which the crate raises after signature/issuer/audience/expiry/nonce checks; all other errors stay IdToken. The pre-existing verifier config is unchanged.

No new test sends a bad signature, wrong audience, wrong issuer or wrong nonce through the re-authentication callback specifically; coverage of those checks rests on the shared code path and the existing sign-in tests.

At HEAD identify_checked verifies the ID token with client.id_token_verifier() and no auth_time hook (grep set_auth_time_verifier_fn in src/oidc.rs: no hits). auth_time is returned beside the identity and judged afterwards by check_auth_time in identify_fresh (absent, too old or too far in the future means not fresh), so a stale auth_time is no longer an ID-token verification failure but a freshness flag, changed deliberately by 0b8aa22 so the account is compared before freshness. Signature, issuer, audience, nonce and expiry still go through the same code as sign-in. The claim's words "inside that verification" no longer describe the code.

verdicts.rationale: Re-authentication and sign-in share identify_checked and the crate verifier; auth_time is added as a verifier hook, not a post-hoc claim read. No reauth-specific negative tests for signature, audience, issuer or nonce exist (EVD-2571, neutral), so the support is by shared code path.

Since 0b8aa22 the auth_time is no longer checked inside the ID-token verification (no verifier hook): identify_checked verifies the token, and check_auth_time judges auth_time afterwards as a freshness flag. The claim's mechanism wording is stale, though the behaviour intent holds (replacement CLM-1767, supported). Fix: retire this claim as superseded by CLM-1767, which states the current verification and auth_time judgement.

claims.statement: The re-authentication callback verifies the ID token fully (signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry) through the same identify_checked code as sign-in, then judges the verified token's auth_time: a missing, older-than-window or far-future auth_time makes the answer not fresh.
claims.source: Issue #775 requirement: full ID-token validation; replaces CLM-1738 after 0b8aa22 moved the auth_time judgement out of the verifier

evidence.summary: identify and identify_fresh both call identify_checked, which exchanges the code with the PKCE verifier and calls id_token.claims(&client.id_token_verifier(), &nonce) (crate verification of signature, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry), then returns the claims' auth_time. identify_fresh passes it to check_auth_time, which returns an error for an absent auth_time, one older than REAUTH_AUTH_TIME_WINDOW (5 minutes) or later than REAUTH_CLOCK_SKEW (60 s) ahead, and identify_fresh reports that as fresh=false. http/oidc.rs:386 uses identify_fresh for the re-authentication callback and identify for sign-in.

check_auth_time rejects an absent auth_time, accepts now and the window edge, rejects one second past the window, accepts the skew edge and rejects one second past it. Passes in both modes. No test sends a bad signature, audience, issuer or nonce through the re-authentication callback specifically; those checks rest on the shared code path.

verdicts.rationale: Shared identify_checked verification plus a tested post-verification auth_time judgement; the callback uses identify_fresh. Residual: no reauth-specific negative tests for signature, audience, issuer or nonce.

claims.statement: The session id and the changeset handle are capabilities (holding the value lets the holder act on the session or changeset, with the right key), and the span never exports either raw: only a digest.
claims.source: Maintainer requirement: check whether Mcp-Session-Id and the changeset handle are bearer capabilities; if so record a digest, never the raw value

evidence.summary: Both are capabilities. The session id is a UUIDv4 (rmcp) and sessions.rs comments say a session id lets its holder use the session; bind_session binds it to the opening key, so the key is also needed. The changeset handle is a random UUID (gen_random_uuid) and resolve_changeset requires owning key or admin. So each is bearer-like but key-gated; a raw export would hand out a handle the maintainer asked to protect.

Passed. The Debug text of every exported span, under each filter, contains neither the raw session id nor the raw changeset handle; call_tool records only digest_token output for both (mod.rs:392-407).

Both ids are key-gated capabilities and the span carries only a deterministic unkeyed digest (stable across replicas, domain-separated, 64 bits of an id that is a 122-bit random UUID), with a test asserting no raw value in any exported span.

verdicts.rationale: Both ids are key-gated capabilities and only digests are exported; the two children hold and the test finds no raw value.

claims.statement: The digests are stable across processes and replicas: they are an unkeyed SHA-256 of a fixed domain and the value, with no per-process state.
claims.source: Maintainer requirement: a digest stable within a process and ideally across replicas; PR body: 'every replica gives the same token'

evidence.summary: digest_token is a pure function: SHA-256 over domain bytes, a 0 byte and the value, first 8 bytes as hex. No salt, key, counter or process state, so every process and replica computes the same token for the same id.

verdicts.rationale: digest_token is pure and unkeyed, so it is the same in every process and replica.

claims.statement: PR statement: each digest is the first 16 hex digits of SHA-256(kind, 0x00, value), and the kind prefix stops a session token matching a changeset token.
claims.source: PR body: 'Each is the first 16 hex digits of `SHA-256(kind, 0x00, value)` ... The kind prefix stops a session token matching a changeset token.'

evidence.summary: Code hashes domain, 0x00, value and keeps bytes [..8] as lowercase 2-digit hex (16 digits). The test asserts a 16-char token and digest_token("session","x") != digest_token("changeset","x"). Test pins length and domain separation but not an exact known-answer value.

verdicts.rationale: The code matches the stated construction and the test pins length and domain separation.

claims.statement: PR statement: a changeset records its catalog only after the ownership check, so a handle the caller does not own reveals no catalog.
claims.source: PR body: 'A changeset records its catalog only after the ownership check, so a stranger's handle reveals nothing.'

evidence.summary: note_catalog sits after the `if !self.offers(&catalog) || !(own || admin) { return Err(unknown()) }` check, so a stranger's handle returns before it. Earlier early returns (unknown handle, catalog not selected) also precede it. No test covers a stranger's handle recording no catalog; the claim rests on code order.

verdicts.rationale: By code order, note_catalog runs only after the ownership and offers check. No test covers the stranger case.

evidence.summary: send builds the router and awaits oneshot plus body read inline (no spawn). claims.statement: Before the change the whoami test installed its subscriber without refreshing tracing's callsite interest cache, so a sqlx::query callsite cached as disabled by another thread could leave it counting nothing.
claims.source: PR body: "the test counted rows through a subscriber without refreshing tracing's callsite interest cache, so a `sqlx::query` callsite cached as disabled by another test thread could leave it counting nothing."

evidence.summary: test_tracing.rs documents the mechanism: a thread with no subscriber can register a callsite as never while a scoped subscriber is alive. At origin/main the whoami test called set_default and then sent the request with no rebuild_interest_cache (the diff's removed lines). The test's warm-up request ran before the subscriber was installed, so it registered callsites under another default. This shows the race is possible; the flake was never reproduced, so it is not shown to be the actual cause.

verdicts.rationale: The pre-change test lacked the refresh and the repository's own test_tracing docs describe the race, so "could leave it counting nothing" is established as possible.

claims.statement: The sweep never deletes a folder whose path appears in the command line of a running process.
claims.source: Issue #1078: 'not used by any running process'

status.reason: Restated more precisely as CLM-2039 after PR review: it now covers the incomplete-snapshot rule and its residue.

evidence.summary: Rerun by me: 9 passed. The test gives one cmdline containing --user-data-dir=<live path> and asserts only the other old folder is selected. The assertion reads as the claim says.

sweep_stale re-runs stale_folders with the real cmdlines from all_cmdlines (every numeric /proc entry's cmdline) and deletes only that result; a byte-substring match of the folder path anywhere in a cmdline keeps it. Weakness (not blocking): all_cmdlines fails open. If /proc cannot be listed it returns an empty Vec, and a per-process cmdline that cannot be read is skipped, so such folders would be treated as unused. A process that starts after the read is also not seen, but the folder must already be a day old.

The sweep thread reads all_cmdlines() and passes it to sweep_stale, which returns 0 when the list is empty and otherwise deletes only folders that stale_folders keeps after the in-use check (path bytes found in any cmdline). This closes the earlier fail-open when /proc is unreadable; a single unreadable process cmdline is still skipped (the list stays non-empty because this process itself is readable).

Rerun by me on HEAD: 10 passed, 0 failed. The new test sweeps an old okf-ui-browser- folder with an empty cmdline list and asserts 0 removed and the folder still exists; the in-use test still asserts the live folder is not selected.

verdicts.rationale: A folder whose path is in any readable cmdline is dropped from the delete set, and the test asserts it. Caveat recorded as neutral EVD-3596: unreadable /proc fails open.
In-use check unchanged, and the fail-open on an unreadable /proc is now closed by the empty-cmdlines guard with a passing test.

claims.statement: The sweep never follows or deletes a symlink named like a leftover folder.
claims.source: Issue #1078: 'never follow symlinks'

evidence.summary: Rerun by me: passed. A 2-day-old okf-ui-browser-link symlink to an old directory is not selected by stale_folders, and sweep_stale returns 0. The test's last assert (target file still exists) is weak because the target is named "precious" and has no prefix, so it would survive anyway; the found.is_empty() and removed == 0 asserts are what show the symlink is skipped.

Selection uses fs::symlink_metadata (does not follow), and requires metadata.is_dir(), which is false for a symlink, so a symlink is never selected, hence never passed to remove_dir_all. remove_dir_all does not follow symlinks inside a folder (std documents this). A folder swapped for a symlink between selection and delete would be unlinked, not followed.

verdicts.rationale: symlink_metadata plus is_dir excludes symlinks from selection; the test asserts none selected and zero removed.

verdicts.rationale: Selection requires metadata.uid() == uid with the effective uid; the test shows a different uid selects nothing. A truly foreign-owned folder is not exercised (needs root).

claims.statement: The flake was caused by the #whoami wait being met by a console booted on the stored key, which only appears when the session fetch at boot fails or the navigation is slow, and which the new exact wait then outlasts until the account session's page shows.
claims.source: PR body: "Under load the wait was met by a console booted on the key" and "the stale console only appears when the session fetch at boot fails or the navigation is slow"

status.reason: The PR body and changelog no longer assert that the exact wait outlasts a key-booted console (commit 9a39160b); replaced by claims on the corrected wording. Its refutation stays in the history.

evidence.locator: src/http/ui/js/main.js:170-190 (boot) and grep of boot()/location.reload in src/http/ui/js
evidence.summary: boot() runs once per document load (called only at line 190) and picks either the session branch (key dropped, whoami = "carol - read") or the stored-key branch (whoami = key text). Nothing switches a key-booted console to the account session without a new document load (no location.reload; the login-form handler and the 401 handler never adopt a cookie session). So if the console booted on the key, #whoami stays "console-carol - read" and wait_text_is("#whoami","carol - read") would time out, not wait it out. The stated mechanism cannot be cured by the exact wait; the exact wait helps only if the key text is on a document that is then replaced.

verdicts.rationale: boot() decides once per document: a console that booted on the stored key keeps the key's #whoami text for the life of that document, so the exact wait would time out rather than outlast it. The description's mechanism (key-booted console, exact wait rides it out) is therefore self-contradictory. Fix: replace the causal sentences in the PR body and changelog with what is shown (the substring wait could be met by key text), and before claiming the flake fixed, either poll localStorage okf.key until null under a bound (the issue's first option), or add failure diagnostics (#whoami text, location.href, GET /api/v1/session status) to the journey to identify which document the key text came from.

claims.statement: The state wait in merge-reviewed.sh ends within AGENTIC_STATE_WAIT + 2 s + agentic_kill_after + agentic_reap_after (72 s with the defaults 60, 5, 5), even when a state lookup stalls and ignores TERM, and the stalled lookup's process group is stopped, leaving no process running (one that survives KILL is abandoned with a warning by lib.sh).
claims.source: PR #1167 round 3 (review 6091371558): document the wait as a polling budget plus grace and cleanup

evidence.summary: Timing: deadline=floor(t0)+W <= t0+W. agentic_deadline=deadline+1. A lookup starts only if budget=agentic_deadline-floor(r)>0, and gets exactly that budget, so ends < deadline+2 (floor loses <1 s). After a sleep the loop ends at <= deadline, and left<=0 breaks, so no lookup starts later. Timeout -> agentic_stop_group: TERM, <=kill_after s wait, KILL, <=reap_after s wait (only when KILL survived), then returns; leader gone -> wait returns at once; survivor is disowned/warned. Total < W+2+kill_after+reap_after = 72 s. Test with TERM-ignoring 20 s lookup bounded (below). Only theoretical caveat: 0.1 s tick loops add ms of fork overhead, absorbed by the strict '<' slack except at pathological clock phase.

verdicts.rationale: Traced floor-clock, +1 s grace, TERM/KILL/reap waits: end < W+2+5+5; leader dead after KILL is reaped at once; survivors abandoned. Only ms-scale tick overhead caveat.

claims.source: Reviewer's point on PR #1211: reading second back does not prove the reader tab's pending first-account requests finished; changelog 'Review round'

evidence.summary: wait_fetches_settled is the first statement of the helper; track_fetches follows wait_worker in both journeys. TRACK_FETCHES wraps window.fetch with a counter decremented in finally; the wait needs the counter 0 on two reads 100 ms apart, up to WAIT, else panics. The reader's only /api/v1 requests are page fetches (src/http/read/js/api.js:48,92 are the only fetch calls of /api/v1; sw.js fetches only shell files and the page's own requests), so no /api/v1 request of the reader bypasses the count. The page's navigation from open_reader is hash-only so the wrapper persists. Not run by me.

verdicts.rationale: Code and the set of /api/v1 request sources show the wait covers the reader's pending requests.

claims.statement: The two journeys still keep the reader tab open and do not drive it between track_fetches and the second tab's sign-in: track_fetches only wraps window.fetch and the wait only reads a counter.
claims.source: Changelog 'Review round': "The reader tab stays open and untouched, so what each journey tests is unchanged."

evidence.summary: The only changes to the two journeys are one ui.track_fetches() line each, after wait_worker and before open_reader; all later steps are unchanged. The helper's added wait only evals a counter read on the reader page.

verdicts.rationale: Only one added line per journey, and it does not navigate or click.

claims.statement: The test the_second_sign_in_waits_for_the_readers_pending_requests holds a reader GET /api/v1/session, asserts fetches_settle_within(1.5 s) is false while it is held, releases it, asserts the wait then returns true, and then runs sign_in_second_in_another_tab.
claims.source: Changelog 'Review round': "holds a request in the reader and asserts the wait does not return while it is held and does once it is released"

evidence.summary: Read the assertions: hold_next(GET, /api/v1/session) installed before track_fetches, so the held fetch is counted; assert!(!fetches_settle_within(1500 ms)); release_held; assert!(fetches_settle_within(10 s)); then sign_in_second_in_another_tab(ui). The assertions would fail with a no-op wait. I did not run the test; the author's report of a failing run with the wait made a no-op and passing in 4 store passes is theirs only.

verdicts.rationale: The assertions in the test body match the statement and fail under a no-op wait; I read them but did not run the test.
